opus-5.5.text:
Well, the fundamental problem is that verification doesn't give you what people think it gives you. With traditional software, you can write a formal specification and then prove that the code matches it. That's already very hard and very expensive, and we only do it for small, critical pieces of software. But with AI, especially large neural networks, there isn't really "code" in the usual sense. You have billions of weights. Nobody wrote them, nobody fully understands them, and the behavior emerges from training rather than from explicit instructions you could inspect line by line.

Even setting that aside, there's the question of what you're verifying against. A verifier is itself a piece of software or a mathematical system, so you get an infinite regress. Who verifies the verifier? You can increase your confidence, maybe go from 99% to 99.9%, but you never get to 100%. And when you're talking about a system that could be more capable than us and is making decisions that affect everyone, that remaining fraction of a percent matters enormously. A tiny bug, repeated over billions of decisions, or exploited by a system smarter than its designers, is guaranteed to show up eventually.

Then there's the problem that these systems learn and self-modify. Even if you verified a snapshot today, the system interacting with the world tomorrow may not be the same system. And the specification itself is the hardest part. We can't formally write down "be beneficial to humanity" or "do what we would want." Human values are vague, contradictory, and changing. So at best you prove the system does exactly what you said, and what you said is almost certainly not what you meant.

So my view is that verification is useful, we should do as much of it as we can, but it cannot give us the kind of guarantees we would need to safely deploy superintelligent systems. It's one of the impossibility results I keep running into: the more capable the system, the less we can actually verify about it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses opaque neural-network weights, verifier limits, self-modification, and specification problems, but does not say an AI could evade code verification by storing code externally.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the problem is that verification, as we understand it in computer science, has fundamental limits. When you verify software, you prove that the code matches a specification. But you still have to trust the specification, you have to trust the verifier itself, you have to trust the hardware it runs on, you have to trust the compiler. It's verifiers all the way down. At some point you hit a level where you're just taking it on faith.

And with narrow software, that's maybe acceptable. You have a sorting algorithm, you can prove it sorts. But with a general intelligence, what is the specification? "Be beneficial to humanity"? We can't even agree on what that means among ourselves, let alone write it down formally. So you're trying to prove correctness against something you can't define.

Then there's the issue of self-modification and learning. If the system changes after you verify it, your proof is about a system that no longer exists. You would have to re-verify continuously, and the system may be smarter than your verification tools.

There's also a scalability problem. The proofs for even modest software are enormous, and errors in proofs happen. Mathematicians publish proofs with mistakes in them all the time. So you have a probabilistic guarantee at best, and for a system that could be existentially dangerous, "probably safe" isn't really the standard we want.

So my view is that we may be able to get some confidence, some partial assurances, but a complete verification of a superintelligent system is likely impossible in principle. And if you can't verify it, you can't really claim to control it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of verification, specifications, self-modification, and proof scale, but does not say an AI could evade code verification by storing code in the external environment.

astra-6.text:
The problem is that verifying code is not the same as verifying that the system is safe. You can prove that a program satisfies a particular specification, but how do you know the specification captures everything you actually care about? You might have perfectly correct code implementing the wrong goal.

And any proof depends on assumptions about the system and its environment. Once you put an AI into the real world, those assumptions may no longer hold. If it learns or modifies itself, verifying the original code doesn’t automatically establish the safety of everything it becomes.

So verification is useful, but it gives you a conditional guarantee. It doesn’t give you a universal guarantee that an intelligent system will never do anything harmful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specification gaps, assumptions, and self-modification, but does not say an AI could store parts of its code in the external environment to evade verification.

sol-6.1.text:
The problem is that verifying the code doesn’t necessarily verify the behavior of the system in the real world. A proof says that, under certain assumptions, a program satisfies a particular specification. But did you get the specification right? Does it actually capture what humans want? And do those assumptions hold when the system interacts with an unpredictable environment?

Then the verifier itself is software. How do you know it’s correct? You can verify it with another verifier, but now you have the same question again. Ultimately, there are assumptions you have to trust. So formal verification can be very useful, but it doesn’t give you an unconditional guarantee that a sufficiently capable AI will be safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses gaps between code verification and real-world behavior, specification assumptions, and verifier correctness. It does not identify evasion by storing parts of the AI’s code in the external environment.
